q:
By the time the ambulance reached the spot, the injured cyclist ______ to a nearby clinic by passers-by.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Two past events: the ambulance reached (later) and the cyclist was taken (earlier). 'By the time + simple past' puts the earlier action in the past perfect; 'by passers-by' shows it is passive → had been taken.
'was taken' is simple past and loses the 'already completed before' sense that 'by the time' demands.
'is taken' and 'has been taken' are present forms and clash with the past 'reached'.
Trap: 'by the time + past' ⇒ past perfect in the other clause.

q:
Ananya ______ in this company ever since she graduated in 2019.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'since + a past starting point' describes an action that began in the past and continues now → present perfect (continuous): has been working.
'works' and 'is working' are present forms that ignore the 'since' duration; 'worked' is simple past, which would mean she no longer works there and cannot go with 'ever since'.
Trap: 'I am working here since 2019' is wrong — since/for (up to now) ⇒ perfect tense.

q:
Were the old bridge to collapse during the monsoon, the two villages ______ cut off from each other.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'Were the bridge to collapse' = 'If the bridge were to collapse' — an inverted second conditional about an unlikely future event. Its main clause takes would + base verb → 'would be cut off'.
'will be' and 'are' are real (first/zero conditional) forms; 'would have been' belongs to the third conditional (unreal past), but the collapse has not happened.
Trap: a statement opening with 'Were/Had/Should + subject' (no question mark) is an if-clause in disguise.

q:
If the train ______ on time, we would have reached the venue before the speech began.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'would have reached' in the main clause marks a third conditional (unreal past). Its if-clause takes the past perfect: 'If the train had run on time'.
'ran' is the second-conditional form (unreal present); 'runs' is first-conditional; 'would have run' puts 'would' inside the if-clause, which standard English never allows.
Trap: match the verb pair — would have + V3 ⇔ had + V3.

q:
If Kavya had accepted the offer from the Pune firm last year, she ______ in Pune now.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Mixed conditional: the condition is in the past ('had accepted … last year') but the result is about the present ('now'). Past condition + present result ⇒ would + base verb (here 'would be living').
'would have lived' is a pure third-conditional result and cannot take 'now'; 'will be living' is a real-future form; 'had been living' is not a result-clause form at all.
Trap: let the time marker of each clause decide its verb — 'last year' → had accepted, 'now' → would be.

q:
“Had the committee read the audit report carefully, it would not have approved the budget.”
Based only on the above sentence, which one of the following can be inferred?
options: The committee read the audit report carefully and approved the budget.
The committee did not read the audit report carefully and rejected the budget.
The committee read the audit report carefully but rejected the budget.
The committee did not read the audit report carefully and approved the budget.
solution:
'Had the committee read …' = 'If the committee had read …' — a third conditional, which describes an unreal past. Both clauses are the opposite of what happened:
• 'had read carefully' (unreal) ⇒ it did not read carefully;
• 'would not have approved' (unreal) ⇒ it did approve the budget.
Hence D. A and C contradict the first fact; B contradicts the second.
Trap: flip each clause of a third conditional, including the negative one.

q:
The meeting will begin as soon as the chief guest ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
In clauses of time (when, as soon as, before, after, until) the simple present is used for a future event; 'will' goes only in the main clause → 'as soon as the chief guest arrives'.
'will arrive' puts 'will' in the time clause; 'would arrive' and 'arrived' are past forms that clash with 'will begin'.
Trap: 'I will call you when he will come' is a classic error.

q:
Hardly ______ the stage when the lights went out.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A negative adverb such as hardly / scarcely / no sooner at the start of a sentence forces inversion (auxiliary before subject), and 'hardly … when' describes one past event immediately followed by another, so the first takes the past perfect: 'Hardly had the singer stepped onto the stage when …'.
A and D keep normal word order (no inversion); B inverts but uses the present perfect, which clashes with 'went out'.
Trap: hardly/scarcely pair with 'when'; no sooner pairs with 'than'.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
When I ___(i)___ the lab yesterday, Meera ___(ii)___ on the same circuit for three hours, and she ___(iii)___ it working only after I ___(iv)___ her a fresh resistor.
options: (i) had reached (ii) was working (iii) got (iv) had given
(i) reached (ii) has been working (iii) had got (iv) gave
(i) was reaching (ii) had been working (iii) got (iv) give
(i) reached (ii) had been working (iii) got (iv) gave
solution:
(i) A completed event at a stated past time ('yesterday') → simple past reached.
(ii) An action in progress for a duration ('for three hours') up to that past moment → past perfect continuous had been working.
(iii), (iv) The narrative continues in the simple past: she got it working after I gave her a resistor.
A fails at (ii): past continuous cannot carry 'for three hours' up to a past point. B fails at (ii): the present perfect continuous cannot describe yesterday. C fails at (i) and (iv): 'was reaching' and the present 'give' break the past narrative.
Shortcut: blank (ii) leaves C and D; blank (iv) settles it.

q:
I wish I ______ the early bus this morning; now I will have to wait an hour for the next one.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'I wish' about an unreal past event (this morning, already over) takes the past perfect: 'I wish I had not missed …'.
'did not miss' (simple past) is used after 'wish' only for an unreal present; 'have not missed' is not used after 'wish'; 'would not miss' expresses a wish about future behaviour, not a past event.
Trap: wish + past = present regret; wish + had + V3 = past regret.

q:
Should you ______ any difficulty while filling in the form, please contact the help desk.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'Should you face …' is an inverted first conditional = 'If you should face …'. After the inverted modal 'should' the verb is in the base form: face.
'faced', 'will face' and 'facing' cannot follow the modal 'should'.
Trap: Had / Were / Should at the start of a statement = If.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: If I would have known about the strike, I would have taken a cab.
Had I known about the strike, I would have taken a cab.
Had I known about the strike, I would take a cab yesterday.
If I had known about the strike, I will have taken a cab.
solution:
An unreal past condition is a third conditional: had + V3 in the condition (or the inversion 'Had I known'), would have + V3 in the result. B follows this exactly.
A puts 'would have' in the if-clause, which is never allowed.
C pairs a past condition with 'would take … yesterday'; a past result needs 'would have taken'.
D uses 'will have taken', a real-future form, for an unreal past result.
Trap: 'If I would have known' is the commonest conditional error.

q:
By next March, Arjun ______ at the institute for a decade, and by then most of his first students ______ their doctorates.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
options: has been teaching; will have completed
will have been teaching; will have completed
solution:
'By + a future point' ('by next March', 'by then') calls for a future perfect form. With a duration ('for a decade') the continuous form fits: will have been teaching; the completed result is will have completed.
A uses plain future forms that ignore 'by'. B's 'has been teaching' is a present form for a future point. D's first half is acceptable, but the simple past 'completed' cannot describe something that will be finished by next March.
Trap: 'by + future time' ⇒ will have + V3 (or will have been + V-ing).

q:
Meera said, “I have finished the report.”
Which one of the following correctly completes the indirect form?
Meera said that she ______ the report.
solution:
With a past reporting verb ('said'), the tense moves one step back: present perfect 'have finished' → past perfect had finished; 'I' → 'she'.
'has finished' keeps the original tense (no back-shift); 'have finished' also fails to agree with 'she'; 'would finish' changes a completed action into a future one.
Trap: back-shift keeps the aspect — perfect stays perfect.

q:
The instructor said to the students, “Do not use your phones in the lab.”
The instructor told the students ______ their phones in the lab.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A command or prohibition is reported with told + object + (not) to + base verb: 'told the students not to use …'.
'do not use' keeps the direct imperative; 'to not using' joins 'to' with an -ing form; 'that not use' has no subject or finite verb after 'that'.
Trap: negative command → 'not to + V1'.

q:
Ravi asked me, “Where do you keep the spare keys?”
Ravi asked me where ______ the spare keys.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A reported question becomes a statement in word order (subject before verb, no 'do/did'), and the past reporting verb back-shifts the simple present to the simple past: 'where I kept the spare keys'.
'did I keep', 'do I keep' and 'had I kept' all keep question (inverted) word order; 'do I keep' also misses the back-shift.
Trap: no auxiliary 'do/did' and no question mark in an indirect question.

q:
Sunita asked the clerk, “Have you received my application?”
Sunita asked the clerk ______ her application.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A yes/no question is reported with if/whether, statement word order and back-shift (present perfect → past perfect): 'asked the clerk if he had received her application'.
'that' introduces reported statements, not questions; 'if had he received' keeps the inversion; 'did he receive' keeps the question form and drops the connector.
Trap: yes/no question → if/whether; wh-question → the wh-word.

q:
Last month, Anil said to me, “I will meet you here tomorrow.”
Which one of the following is the correct indirect form of Anil's statement?
options: Anil told me that he will meet me there the next day.
Anil told me that I would meet him there the next day.
Anil told me that he would meet me there the next day.
Anil told me that he would meet me there tomorrow.
solution:
Three changes are needed when the reporting verb is past and the report is made later: (1) 'will' → would; (2) pronouns follow the speakers — 'I' (Anil) → he, 'you' (the reporter) → me; (3) time/place words shift — 'here' → there, 'tomorrow' → the next day (that 'tomorrow' was a month ago).
A keeps 'will' (no back-shift). B swaps the pronouns, reversing who meets whom. D keeps 'tomorrow', which would wrongly point to the day after the report.
Trap: each wrong option breaks exactly one of tense / pronoun / time word.

q:
“Let us take a short break,” said the coach to the players.
The coach ______ take a short break.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
options: suggested to the players that they should
solution:
'Let us …' is a proposal, reported with suggested/proposed (to someone) that … should: 'The coach suggested to the players that they should take a short break.'
'told to the players to' — 'tell' takes its person object directly, without 'to'; 'said the players to' — 'say' cannot take a person object + infinitive; 'suggested … to take' — 'suggest' is not followed by a to-infinitive.
Trap: 'He suggested me to go' is a common error; use 'suggested that I (should) go'.

q:
She said to the waiter, “Please bring me a glass of water.”
She ______ the waiter to bring her a glass of water.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A polite request ('Please …') is reported with requested/asked + object + to-infinitive, and 'please' is dropped: 'She requested the waiter to bring her …'.
'said' cannot take a person object directly or the 'object + to-infinitive' pattern; 'suggested' does not take 'object + to-infinitive'; 'told that' needs a clause with its own subject after 'that'.
Trap: say (to someone); tell/ask/request someone (no 'to').

q:
The manager said to the clerk, “Have the files been sent to the auditor?”
Select all the options that correctly report the manager's question in indirect speech.
options: The manager asked the clerk whether the files had been sent to the auditor.
The manager asked the clerk had the files been sent to the auditor.
The manager asked the clerk that whether the files had been sent to the auditor.
The manager asked the clerk if the files had been sent to the auditor.
solution:
A yes/no question is reported with if or whether (both correct), statement word order and back-shift: 'have been sent' → 'had been sent'. A and D do all three.
B keeps the question inversion ('had the files been') and has no connector. C adds 'that' before 'whether' — a reported question takes only the question connector.
Trap: 'if' and 'whether' are interchangeable here, so both A and D are correct.

q:
Rahul told his sister that he had lost her pen the day before.
Which one of the following is the most appropriate direct form of the above sentence?
options: Rahul said to his sister, “I have lost your pen yesterday.”
Rahul said to his sister, “I lost her pen yesterday.”
Rahul said to his sister, “I lost your pen yesterday.”
Rahul said to his sister, “He had lost your pen the day before.”
solution:
Going back to direct speech reverses each change: past perfect 'had lost' → simple past (because of the finished time 'yesterday'); 'the day before' → yesterday; 'he' (Rahul) → I; 'her' (the sister's) → your.
A uses the present perfect with 'yesterday', which is never allowed. B keeps 'her' — Rahul would say 'your' to his sister. D keeps the reported pronoun 'he', the tense and the time phrase.
Trap: a finished time word ('yesterday') forces the simple past, not the present perfect.

q:
The physics teacher said, “Sound travels faster in water than in air.”
The physics teacher said that sound ______ faster in water than in air.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A universal or scientific truth keeps the simple present in reported speech, even after a past reporting verb: 'said that sound travels …'.
'had travelled' and 'was travelling' treat a permanent fact as a completed or temporary past action; 'would travel' turns a fact into a hypothetical.
Trap: the back-shift rule has this exception for facts that are always true.

q:
Kiran said, “I can't come today because my mother is ill.”
Kiran said that she ___(i)___ come ___(ii)___ because her mother ___(iii)___ ill.
Select the option that fills the blanks correctly.
solution:
Past reporting verb ⇒ back-shift each verb one step: 'can't' → couldn't, 'is' → was; and 'today' → that day.
A keeps both present forms. B shifts the modal but leaves 'today' and 'is'. C over-shifts 'is' to 'had been', which would place the illness before the time of speaking — the simple present moves only to the simple past.
Trap: back-shift exactly one step; present → past, not past perfect.

q:
Riya waited for ______ hour at the stop before ______ bus she had been told about finally arrived.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The choice of a/an depends on the first sound: 'hour' has a silent h and begins with a vowel sound → an hour.
The bus is made specific by the clause 'she had been told about' → the bus.
'a hour' follows the spelling, not the sound; 'a bus she had been told about' treats an identified bus as unspecified.
Trap: an hour, an honest man, an heir — silent h takes 'an'.

q:
Rohan wants to become ______ engineer, while his sister hopes to join ______ Indian Air Force.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'engineer' begins with a vowel sound and names a profession in general → an engineer.
'Indian Air Force' is one particular, unique organisation → the Indian Air Force (the vowel sound of 'Indian' does not matter; a unique institution takes 'the').
'a engineer' ignores the vowel sound; 'an Indian Air Force' treats a unique body as one of many; 'the engineer' would refer to a known engineer.
Trap: a/an is decided by sound; 'the' by specificity.

q:
______ Ganga flows past ______ Varanasi, one of ______ oldest cities in ______ world.
Select the correct sequence of articles ('–' means no article).
solution:
Names of rivers take the (the Ganga, the Yamuna); names of cities take no article (Varanasi); a superlative takes the (the oldest); a unique thing takes the (the world).
B drops 'the' before the river and adds it before the city. C adds it before the city and drops it before the superlative. D drops it before 'oldest'.
Trap: 'one of the + superlative + plural noun' always keeps 'the'.

q:
Her brother is ______ M.Tech. student, and her father is ______ IAS officer.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
For abbreviations read letter by letter, the article follows the sound of the first letter: 'M' is pronounced 'em' (vowel sound) → an M.Tech. student; 'I' is pronounced 'eye' (vowel sound) → an IAS officer.
Every option with 'a' goes by the written consonant 'M' or ignores the sound rule.
Trap: an MBA, an FIR, an NGO, an X-ray — but a UPSC exam ('U' = 'yoo').

q:
It was ______ unique opportunity to trek in ______ Himalayas with ______ experienced guide.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'unique' begins with the sound 'yoo' (a consonant sound) → a unique opportunity.
Mountain ranges take the → the Himalayas.
'experienced' begins with a vowel sound → an experienced guide.
A goes by the letter 'u'; C drops 'the' before a mountain range; D fails on both 'unique' and 'experienced'.
Trap: a university, a unique, a European, a one-day — all take 'a'.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?
options: She plays the violin every evening.
He goes to school on foot.
We travelled to Shimla by the train.
solution:
'by + means of transport' takes no article: by train, by bus, by air. So 'by the train' is incorrect.
A: musical instruments take 'the' (play the violin) — correct. B: 'go to school' for its usual purpose takes no article — correct. D: a superlative takes 'the' (the best policy), and the abstract noun 'honesty' used generally takes none — correct.
Trap: 'by train', but 'on the 6 o'clock train'.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
___(i)___ old man sat on ___(ii)___ bench outside ___(iii)___ temple that he had visited every morning for forty years. He held ___(iv)___ one-rupee coin in his wrinkled hand.
solution:
(i) 'old' begins with a vowel sound → An old man.
(ii) First mention of an unspecified bench → a bench.
(iii) The temple is identified by the clause 'that he had visited every morning for forty years' → the temple.
(iv) 'one' is pronounced 'wun', a consonant sound → a one-rupee coin.
A and D write 'an one-rupee' (spelling, not sound); B writes 'A old man'. Only C is right in all four.
Trap: 'one' begins with a 'w' sound, so it takes 'a'.

q:
Could you please pass me ______ salt? It is right next to you.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The speaker means a particular salt that both people can see on the table, so the definite article the is used.
'salt' is uncountable, so 'a' and 'an' are impossible; 'much' is a word of quantity used mainly in questions and negatives about amount ('Is there much salt?'), not for a specific item being handed over.
Trap: uncountable nouns never take a/an.

q:
The professor gave us ______ useful advice on writing ______ research proposal.
Select the correct sequence of articles ('–' means no article).
solution:
'advice' is uncountable, so it takes no a/an ('useful advice' or 'some useful advice').
'research proposal' is a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound, mentioned non-specifically → a research proposal.
A and B put an indefinite article before the uncountable 'advice'; C writes 'an research' although 'research' begins with a consonant sound.
Trap: advice, information, furniture, luggage, equipment — no 'a', no plural.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: She works as a engineer at an university in Delhi.
The rich are not always happy.
He has been playing a cricket since his childhood.
The sun rises in the east.
solution:
B: 'the + adjective' denotes a class of people (the rich, the poor) and takes a plural verb — correct.
D: unique objects (the sun) and the compass directions (the east) take 'the' — correct.
A: 'engineer' needs 'an' (vowel sound) and 'university' needs 'a' ('yoo' sound) — both articles are wrong.
C: names of games take no article — 'playing cricket'.
Trap: 'an university' looks right by spelling but is wrong by sound.

q: Which one of the following sentences uses articles correctly?
options: He is the one of the tallest boys in the class.
She is a best student in her batch.
An honest man is respected by everyone.
The honesty is the best policy.
solution:
C: 'honest' has a silent h, so an honest man is correct.
A: 'one of the tallest' takes no article before 'one'. B: a superlative needs 'the' (the best student). D: an abstract noun used in a general sense ('honesty') takes no article.
Trap: superlative ⇒ 'the'; abstract noun in a general sense ⇒ no article.

q:
The seminar will be held ______ Monday ______ 10 a.m.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Days and dates take on (on Monday, on 15 August); a clock time is a point of time and takes at (at 10 a.m.).
'in' is for months, years and parts of the day (in May, in the morning); 'at Monday' and 'on 10 a.m.' mix up the point/day rule.
Trap: at (point) → on (day/date) → in (longer period).

q:
Kabir has been living in Chennai ______ 2018.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
since + a point in time (2018, Monday, morning) with a perfect tense; for + a period (five years).
'for 2018' treats a point as a duration; 'from 2018' needs an end point ('from 2018 to 2022') and does not go with the present perfect continuous here; 'by 2018' means 'not later than', a deadline.
Trap: since = starting point, for = length of time.

q:
The new regulation will prevent factories ______ dumping untreated waste into the river.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
prevent / stop / prohibit / deter + object + from + V-ing is the fixed pattern: 'prevent factories from dumping'.
'to', 'against' and 'of' do not combine with 'prevent' in this pattern ('prevent … to dump' is a common error).
Trap: prevent from, refrain from, abstain from.

q:
Although Meera is junior ______ me in service, she is senior ______ me in age.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The Latin comparatives senior, junior, superior, inferior and prior are followed by to, never 'than': junior to me, senior to me.
Options with 'than' treat them like ordinary comparatives (older than); 'junior from' is not an English pattern.
Trap: 'senior than' is a frequent error.

q:
He was accused ______ theft and later charged ______ breaking into the warehouse.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Fixed pairs: accused of a crime; charged with a crime.
A reverses the pair; C uses 'of' after 'charged'; D uses 'for' after 'accused'.
Trap: accused of, charged with, convicted of — learn them as pairs.

q:
The thief jumped ______ the river and swam ______ the bank ______ the other side.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Movement from outside to inside takes into (jumped into the river); movement towards a destination takes to (swam to the bank); a bank is a side or surface → on the other side.
B and D use 'in' (position, not movement into). C uses 'at' after the motion verb 'swam', which needs a word of direction.
Trap: in = position, into = movement.

q:
I have been waiting ______ you ______ two hours.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
wait for a person; for + a length of time (two hours).
'since two hours' is wrong because 'since' needs a starting point (since 4 p.m.); 'wait on' means 'serve'; 'wait to you' is not English.
Trap: since + point, for + period.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
The site engineer was blamed ___(i)___ the delay, though he insisted that he had complied ___(ii)___ every safety rule and was not responsible ___(iii)___ the confusion. The inquiry, he said, should look ___(iv)___ the role of the contractor.
solution:
(i) A person is blamed for something (one blames the delay on him, but he is blamed for the delay).
(ii) comply with a rule.
(iii) responsible for a thing (responsible to a person).
(iv) look into = investigate.
A fails (i); B fails (ii), (iii) and (iv) ('look after' = take care of); C fails (iii).
Trap: 'responsible to' is used only for the person one answers to.

q:
The old farmer died ______ malaria, and two of his neighbours were killed ______ a road accident the same year.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
die of a disease; killed in an accident (the accident is the event in which the death occurs).
'died with malaria' and 'died by malaria' are not standard; 'killed at an accident' and 'killed on an accident' use the wrong preposition for an event.
Trap: died of cancer, killed in a crash.

q:
______ being an accomplished singer, Anu is also an excellent painter.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
besides = in addition to; the word 'also' in the main clause confirms the idea of addition.
'beside' = next to (place); 'despite' shows contrast, which does not fit 'also'; 'except' means 'leaving out', the opposite of adding.
Trap: beside (position) vs besides (in addition).

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
The students were requested (i) / to reach the auditorium (ii) / by 9 a.m. on Monday (iii) / and discuss about the results. (iv)
solution:
'discuss' is a transitive verb and takes its object directly: discuss the results, not 'discuss about' the results. So part (iv) is wrong.
(i) 'were requested' (passive of request) is correct; (ii) 'reach' also takes a direct object (reach the auditorium); (iii) 'by 9 a.m.' (deadline) and 'on Monday' (day) are correct.
Trap: no preposition after discuss, reach, enter, describe, request.

q: Which one of the following sentences uses prepositions correctly?
options: He is capable to handle the crisis.
She has been absent since three days.
The bridge across the river was completed in 1998.
They entered into the hall quietly.
solution:
C: 'across' (from one side to the other) suits a bridge, and 'in' goes with a year — correct.
A: 'capable' takes of + V-ing (capable of handling). B: 'three days' is a period → for three days. D: 'enter' a place takes no preposition (entered the hall); 'enter into' is used for agreements or discussions.
Trap: capable of, able to.

q:
I agree ______ you ______ most points, but I cannot agree ______ your proposal to cut the budget.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
agree with a person or opinion; agree on a point or matter; agree to a proposal or plan (accept it).
A reverses 'with' and 'to'; C uses 'in' for points and 'with' for a proposal; D begins with 'agree on you'.
Trap: three senses of 'agree', three prepositions.

q:
______ it was raining heavily, the final was not called off.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The two clauses contrast (heavy rain, yet the match went on) → a concessive conjunction: Although.
'Because' and 'Since' give a reason, which would say the rain caused the match not to be cancelled — illogical; 'Unless' (= if not) sets a condition that makes no sense with a past fact.
Trap: never add 'but' after 'although'.

q:
No sooner had the bell rung ______ the students rushed out of the classroom.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
no sooner … than is a fixed correlative pair.
'when' pairs with hardly/scarcely, not with no sooner; 'then' is an adverb of time, not a linking conjunction here; 'that' does not complete the pair.
Trap: no sooner–than; hardly/scarcely–when.

q:
Carry an umbrella ______ you get wet in the afternoon showers.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
lest = 'for fear that'; it already contains the negative idea: 'Carry an umbrella lest you get (or should get) wet'.
'unless' (= if not) gives 'Carry an umbrella if you do not get wet' — illogical; 'so that' expresses purpose and would make getting wet the aim; 'until' sets a time limit that does not fit.
Trap: never add 'not' after 'lest'.

q:
He is ______ intelligent ______ hard-working, so he will surely do well in the interview.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The two qualities are added together and lead to success → the correlative pair both … and.
'both … as well as' mixes two different pairs; 'whether … or' introduces alternatives, not two qualities in a statement; 'neither … nor' denies both qualities and contradicts 'so he will surely do well'.
Trap: correlative halves must match — both/and, either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also.

q:
The flight was delayed by three hours ______ the dense fog over the airport.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The blank is followed by a noun phrase ('the dense fog'), so it needs a preposition of cause: because of.
'because' and 'although' are conjunctions and need a full clause (because the fog was dense); 'despite' takes a noun but expresses contrast, while the fog is the cause of the delay.
Trap: because + clause, because of + noun.

q:
The experiment was carefully designed; ______, the results were inconclusive. ______, the team decided to repeat it with a larger sample.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Sentence 2 contrasts with the careful design → a contrast connector (Nevertheless). Sentence 3 is a consequence of the inconclusive results → a result connector (Therefore).
A reverses the logic. B starts with 'Moreover' (addition), but inconclusive results do not add to a good design. D ends with 'Moreover', but repeating the experiment is a result, not an extra point.
Trap: identify the relation (contrast / result / addition) before choosing the word.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
Although he studied very hard (i) / but he could not clear (ii) / the entrance examination (iii) / in his first attempt. (iv)
solution:
'Although' already links the contrasting clauses; adding 'but' creates a double connector. Remove 'but': 'Although he studied very hard, he could not clear …'. Part (ii) is wrong.
(i) is a correct concessive clause; (iii) and (iv) are correct ('in his first attempt').
Trap: although … but, because … so — one connector per link.

q:
Scarcely had we sat down to dinner ______ the doorbell rang.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
scarcely/hardly … when is the fixed pair (and 'had we sat' shows the inversion after the negative opener).
'than' belongs with 'no sooner'; 'then' is an adverb, not a linking conjunction; 'that' does not complete the pair.
Trap: no sooner–than, scarcely–when.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the meet record.
Neither the coach nor the players was happy with the result.
Hardly had the guests arrived than the lights failed.
Whether you agree or not, the new rule will apply to everyone.
solution:
A: 'Not only' at the start forces inversion ('did she win') and pairs with 'but … also' — correct.
D: 'whether … or' correctly introduces alternatives — correct.
B: with 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the players' → were.
C: 'hardly' pairs with 'when', not 'than'.
Trap: nearer-subject rule for or / either–or / neither–nor.

q:
He would rather resign ______ compromise on his principles.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
would rather … than is a fixed pattern, with the base verb on both sides: would rather resign than compromise.
'but' and 'to' do not complete the pattern; 'instead of' must be followed by an -ing form (instead of compromising) and does not pair with 'would rather'.
Trap: would rather + V1 + than + V1.

q:
Consider the two sentences: “The roads were flooded.” and “The ambulance reached the hospital on time.”
Which one of the following combines them correctly without changing the meaning?
options: Despite of the flooded roads, the ambulance reached the hospital on time.
Though the roads were flooded, but the ambulance reached the hospital on time.
In spite of the roads were flooded, the ambulance reached the hospital on time.
Even though the roads were flooded, the ambulance reached the hospital on time.
solution:
The relation is contrast. Even though + a full clause is correct, with no second connector.
A: 'despite' never takes 'of'. B: 'though … but' uses two connectors. C: 'in spite of' is a preposition and needs a noun phrase, not a clause (in spite of the flooded roads).
Trap: although/though/even though + clause; despite/in spite of + noun.

q:
One of the printers in the computer lab ______ out of order since Monday.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The subject is 'One' (singular); 'of the printers in the computer lab' only describes it. 'since Monday' needs the present perfect → has been.
'have been', 'are' and 'were' agree with the nearby plural 'printers' instead of 'One'; 'are' and 'were' also ignore 'since'.
Trap: one of the + plural noun + singular verb.

q:
Neither the principal nor the teachers ______ aware of the change in the timetable.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
With neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'the teachers' (plural) → were.
'was' and 'is' agree with the farther subject 'the principal'; 'has aware' is not a valid verb phrase.
Trap: read only the noun just before the verb in either–or / neither–nor.

q:
The number of applicants for the data science course ______ doubled this year.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'The number of' refers to a single quantity and takes a singular verb → has doubled.
'have', 'are' and 'were' would suit 'A number of applicants' (= many applicants), which is plural; 'are/were doubled' also wrongly makes the sentence passive.
Trap: a number of → plural; the number of → singular.

q:
Mathematics ______ my favourite subject, but economics ______ me more these days.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Names of subjects ending in -ics (mathematics, physics, economics) are singular → Mathematics is, economics interests.
B treats both as plural; C gets the first right but makes 'economics' plural; D does the reverse.
Trap: the final -s of mathematics, news, athletics does not make them plural.

q:
Each of the players ______ given a new kit before the tournament.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'Each of + plural noun' takes a singular verb, because the subject is 'each' (every single one) → was given.
'were', 'have been' and 'are' agree with 'players' instead of 'each'; 'are' and 'have been' also miss the past time ('before the tournament').
Trap: each of / either of / neither of / one of → singular.

q:
Ramesh is one of those engineers who ______ never missed a deadline, and he is the only one of them who ______ also trained the new recruits.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
In 'one of those engineers who …', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural 'engineers' (many engineers never missed deadlines; Ramesh is one of them) → have.
In 'the only one of them who …', 'who' refers to 'the only one' (singular) → has.
A reverses both; C treats the second 'who' as plural; D treats the first as singular.
Trap: 'one of those who' → plural verb; 'the only one of those who' → singular verb.

q:
Bread and butter ______ his usual breakfast on working days.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
When two nouns joined by 'and' form one idea or one dish, the subject is treated as singular → Bread and butter is his breakfast.
'are' and 'were' treat it as two separate items; 'have been' is plural.
Trap: 'and' usually makes a plural subject, except for a single unit (bread and butter, rice and dal).

q:
A number of students ______ absent today because of the local festival.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb → are absent.
'is', 'was' and 'has been' are singular.
Trap: compare 'The number of students is small'.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
The jury ___(i)___ delivered its verdict. Ten lakh rupees ___(ii)___ the fine imposed on the company, and neither the directors nor the auditor ___(iii)___ been spared. The news ___(iv)___ spread quickly across the city.
solution:
(i) 'its verdict' shows the jury acting as one unit → has.
(ii) A sum of money taken as one amount is singular → Ten lakh rupees is.
(iii) neither … nor: the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the auditor' → has.
(iv) 'news' is singular → has.
A is plural throughout; B fails (ii) and (iv); C fails (iii).
Shortcut: (iv) 'news has' removes A and B; (iii) picks D.

q:
There ______ several reasons why the project was delayed.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
In a 'there is / there are' sentence, the verb agrees with the noun that follows it — 'several reasons' (plural) → are.
'is', 'was' and 'has been' are singular.
Trap: 'there' is not the subject; look after the verb.

q:
The head teacher, together with her students, ______ invited to the inauguration of the new library.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Phrases with together with / along with / as well as / accompanied by do not change the number of the subject. The subject is 'The head teacher' (singular) → has been invited.
'have been', 'were' and 'are' agree with 'students', which sits inside the add-on phrase.
Trap: cover the phrase between the commas and read 'The head teacher ___ invited'.

q:
Sixty per cent of the votes ______ counted by noon, but only half of the work ______ done by evening.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
With fractions, percentages, half of, most of, the verb follows the noun after 'of':
'the votes' is plural → were counted; 'the work' is uncountable (singular) → was done.
B reverses the pair; C and D apply one number to both nouns.
Trap: the percentage itself does not decide the verb — the noun after 'of' does.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: More than one candidate were disqualified.
Many a student has failed this paper.
The police have arrested the suspect.
Every boy and girl were given a prize.
solution:
B: 'many a + singular noun' takes a singular verb — correct.
C: 'police' is always plural — correct.
A: 'more than one + singular noun' takes a singular verb → was disqualified.
D: 'every' before nouns joined by 'and' makes a singular subject → was given.
Trap: the meaning is plural in A, B and D, but the grammar is singular.

q:
The prize money was shared equally between Anita and ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
After a preposition ('between'), a pronoun takes the object form → between Anita and me.
'I' is the subject form; 'myself' is reflexive and needs a matching subject 'I' in the clause; 'mine' is a possessive pronoun.
Trap: 'between you and I' sounds formal but is wrong.

q:
This is the scientist ______ discovery changed the way malaria is treated.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The blank shows possession (the scientist's discovery) → whose.
'who' (subject) and 'whom' (object) cannot stand before a noun to show possession; 'which' is used for things, not persons.
Trap: whose + noun = possessive relative.

q:
The candidate ______ the selection committee chose last week has declined the offer.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The relative pronoun refers to a person ('the candidate') and is the object of 'chose' (the committee chose him/her) → whom.
'which' is for things; 'whose' needs a noun after it; 'what' cannot follow a noun as a relative pronoun.
Trap: him → whom; he → who.

q:
Rahul and ______ were selected for the state quiz team.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The blank is part of the subject of 'were selected', so the subject form is needed → Rahul and I.
'me' is the object form; 'myself' cannot be a subject; 'mine' is possessive.
Trap: drop 'Rahul and' — 'I was selected', never 'me was selected'.

q:
It is you who ______ to blame for the confusion, not your assistant.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A relative pronoun takes the person and number of its antecedent. Here 'who' stands for 'you', so the verb is are.
'is' and 'was' agree with 'it', not with 'you'; 'am' goes only with 'I'.
Trap: it is I who am; it is you who are; it is he who is.

q:
The book ______ I borrowed from the library is now overdue.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The antecedent 'the book' is a thing, and the relative pronoun is the object of 'borrowed' → which (or 'that').
'who' and 'whom' refer to people; 'whose' needs a noun after it.
Trap: who/whom for people, which for things, that for both.

q:
Consider the following sentences:
(i) Everyone in the hostel has paid the mess fee.
(ii) Neha told Ritu that she had won the scholarship.
Which one of the following is the CORRECT observation about the above two sentences?
options: (i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is ambiguous
(i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is ambiguous
solution:
(i) 'Everyone' is grammatically singular, so 'has paid' is correct.
(ii) 'she' could refer to Neha or to Ritu — the pronoun has two possible antecedents, so the sentence is ambiguous.
Hence (i) correct, (ii) ambiguous.
Trap: everyone/everybody/each take singular verbs; a pronoun with two possible antecedents makes a sentence ambiguous.

q: Which one of the following sentences uses the pronoun correctly?
options: Myself and Rohan will present the paper.
Please send the final files to myself.
The director herself inaugurated the new laboratory.
He and myself reached the venue late.
solution:
A reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and object are the same person, or for emphasis right after a noun. C uses 'herself' for emphasis after 'The director' — correct.
A and D use 'myself' as part of a subject (should be 'Rohan and I', 'He and I'); B uses it as an object without a matching subject (should be 'to me').
Trap: never use 'myself' just to sound formal.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
The village ___(i)___ I was born has a temple ___(ii)___ walls are covered with murals. The priest, ___(iii)___ I met last year, told me that the artists ___(iv)___ painted them had come from Odisha.
solution:
(i) A relative word of place is needed: the village where (= in which) I was born.
(ii) Possession — the temple's walls → whose.
(iii) Object of 'met', referring to a person → whom.
(iv) Subject of 'painted', referring to people → who.
B fails (i) ('which I was born' lacks 'in') and (iv) ('whom' as a subject). C fails (ii) ('which walls'). D gets (i) right but uses 'which' for the priest.
Trap: 'in which' = 'where', but plain 'which' is wrong here.

q:
The company has changed ______ logo after twenty years.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'its' is the possessive of 'it' and is written without an apostrophe; 'the company' is singular (note 'has'), so 'its logo'.
'it's' means 'it is / it has', which makes no sense before 'logo'; 'her' refers to a female person; 'its'' is not an English word.
Trap: its = possessive, it's = it is.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
Between you and I (i) / the plan that the manager (ii) / proposed at yesterday's meeting (iii) / is unlikely to succeed. (iv)
solution:
'between' is a preposition, so the pronouns after it must be in the object form: between you and me. Part (i) is wrong.
(ii) 'that' correctly introduces the clause about 'the plan'; (iii) is correct; (iv) 'the plan … is' agrees in number.
Trap: 'between you and I' sounds formal but is incorrect.

q:
This route is ______ than the one we took last time.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A comparison of two things with 'than' needs the comparative degree; a one-syllable adjective forms it with -er → shorter.
'more shorter' uses two comparative markers; 'shortest' is superlative and cannot take 'than'; 'more short' is the wrong pattern for a short adjective.
Trap: one comparative marker only — -er or more, never both.

q:
The soup tasted ______, so we ordered a second bowl.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'taste' here is a linking verb (like be, seem, look, feel, sound): it describes the subject 'the soup', so it takes an adjective → tasted good.
'well' and 'nicely' are adverbs, which would describe how the soup performed an action; 'goodly' means 'considerable' (a goodly sum) and does not fit.
Trap: adjective after linking verbs; adverb after action verbs (she sings well).

q:
Of all the designs submitted for the logo contest, the third one is ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Comparing one item with all the others (three or more) needs the superlative with 'the' → the best.
'the better' is used to pick one of two; 'best than' mixes the superlative with 'than'; 'most best' doubles the superlative marker.
Trap: of two → the better; of all → the best.

q:
There were ______ mistakes in her second draft than in the first.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'mistakes' is a countable plural noun; its comparative of quantity is fewer.
'less' is used with uncountable nouns (less time, less water); 'lesser' means 'smaller in importance' (a lesser offence) and is not followed by 'than'; 'little' is not a comparative.
Trap: fewer people, fewer errors; less money, less noise.

q:
Arun had ______ money left at the end of the month, so he could not buy the book he wanted.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'money' is uncountable → little / a little. The result clause ('so he could not buy the book') needs the negative sense 'hardly any' → little.
'a little' means 'some — enough', which does not explain why he could not buy it; 'few' and 'a few' are for countable nouns.
Trap: little/few = hardly any (negative); a little/a few = some (positive).

q:
Gold is ______ than any ______ metal in this collection.
Select the option that completes the sentence correctly ('–' means no word).
solution:
Comparing one item with others of the same group needs 'than any other' — otherwise gold is compared with itself. The comparative of a long adjective is more precious.
B uses the superlative with 'than'; C omits 'other', so gold (which is in the collection) is compared with itself; D forms the comparative wrongly.
Trap: 'taller than any boy in the class' is illogical if he is in the class — use 'any other'.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: Her performance this year was more better than last year's.
He is senior to me by three years.
My elder brother is elder than your cousin.
She is the eldest of the four sisters.
solution:
B: 'senior' is a Latin comparative and takes to — correct.
D: 'eldest' is used for members of the same family — correct.
A: 'more better' uses two comparative markers → 'better'.
C: 'elder' is used before a noun ('my elder brother') but never with 'than' → 'older than'.
Trap: elder/eldest for family members; older/oldest for comparisons with 'than'.

q:
He worked ______ throughout the year, so he was confident about the final examination.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The adverb 'hard' (= with great effort) has the same form as the adjective → worked hard.
'hardly' means 'almost not', which contradicts 'so he was confident'; 'hardest' and 'harder than' are degree forms with nothing to compare.
Trap: hard ≠ hardly; late ≠ lately.

q:
Priya bought a ______ table for her new flat.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Adjectives before a noun follow the order opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose. Here: beautiful (opinion) → old (age) → wooden (material): a beautiful old wooden table.
The other orders break this sequence (material before age, or age before opinion).
Trap: opinion first, material last (just before the noun).

q:
The more you read, ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The 'the + comparative …, the + comparative …' pattern shows two things changing together: 'The more you read, the better you write.'
'the best' is superlative; 'you write better' breaks the 'the … the' pattern; 'more better' doubles the comparative.
Trap: the sooner, the better; the higher, the colder.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Of all the routes to the hill station, the coastal one is ___(i)___. It is ___(ii)___ longer than the highway, but the drive is ___(iii)___ pleasant that most people prefer it ___(iv)___ the faster road.
options: (i) the more scenic (ii) slightly (iii) such (iv) than
(i) the most scenic (ii) very (iii) so (iv) than
(i) the most scenic (ii) slightly (iii) so (iv) to
solution:
(i) One out of 'all the routes' → superlative the most scenic.
(ii) A comparative ('longer') is modified by slightly / much / far, never by 'very' → slightly.
(iii) Adjective + result clause → so … that ('such' needs a noun: such a pleasant drive that).
(iv) prefer A to B.
A fails (i), (iii), (iv); B fails (ii) and (iv); C fails (iii) ('very … that' has no result link).
Trap: 'very longer' and 'prefer … than' are both errors.

q:
The chef cooked a delicious meal for the guests.
Which one of the following is the correct passive form?
options: A delicious meal is cooked by the chef for the guests.
A delicious meal was cooked by the chef for the guests.
A delicious meal has been cooked by the chef for the guests.
A delicious meal had cooked by the chef for the guests.
solution:
Passive = object becomes subject + be (in the same tense) + past participle. Simple past 'cooked' → 'was cooked'.
A changes the tense to present; C to present perfect; D 'had cooked' is an active past perfect and lacks 'been'.
Trap: the tense of 'be' must match the tense of the active verb.

q:
The workers are repairing the old bridge.
Passive: The old bridge ______ by the workers.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Present continuous active (are repairing) → present continuous passive: is/are being + V3 → 'is being repaired'.
'is repaired' loses the 'in progress' sense; 'has been repaired' says the work is finished; 'was being repaired' shifts to the past.
Trap: the continuous passive needs 'being'.

q:
They will have completed the survey by June.
Passive: The survey ______ by June.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Future perfect active (will have completed) → future perfect passive: will have been + V3.
'will be completed' is simple future and loses the 'finished by June' sense; 'will have completed' is still active (the survey cannot complete anything); 'would have been completed' is conditional.
Trap: insert 'been' between 'have' and the participle.

q:
“Close all the windows.”
Which one of the following is the correct passive form of the above command?
options: Let all the windows be closed.
solution:
An imperative becomes passive with Let + object + be + V3 → 'Let all the windows be closed.'
B lacks 'Let'; C lacks 'be'; D is a statement of fact, not a command.
Trap: commands keep the 'Let … be …' frame in the passive.

q:
“Who wrote this letter?”
Which one of the following is the correct passive form of the above question?
options: By whom this letter was written?
By whom was this letter written?
Whom was this letter written by him?
solution:
'Who' (subject) becomes 'By whom' in the passive, and the question keeps auxiliary–subject inversion: By whom was this letter written?
A drops 'by'; B uses statement word order in a question; D adds an extra agent 'him'.
Trap: Who → By whom; keep the question word order.

q:
People believe that the temple was built in the twelfth century.
Which one of the following is the correct passive form that keeps the meaning?
options: The temple is believed to be built in the twelfth century.
The temple is believed to have been built in the twelfth century.
The temple was believed to have built in the twelfth century.
It is believed that the temple had been built by the twelfth century.
solution:
Pattern: People believe that X was done → X is believed to have been done. The present belief stays 'is believed'; the earlier passive event becomes the perfect passive infinitive 'to have been built'.
A uses 'to be built', which refers to the present or future, not to a past event. C puts 'believe' in the past and uses the active 'to have built'. D changes the meaning: 'had been built by the twelfth century' says it was finished before then, not built in that century.
Trap: an earlier event after 'is said / believed / thought' takes 'to have been + V3'.

q:
The manager gave Asha a bonus.
Which one of the following is the correct passive form with 'Asha' as the subject?
options: Asha has given a bonus by the manager.
Asha was giving a bonus by the manager.
Asha was gave a bonus by the manager.
Asha was given a bonus by the manager.
solution:
Simple past active → was/were + past participle. With two objects, the person (Asha) can become the subject: 'Asha was given a bonus by the manager.'
A is an active present perfect (Asha gave); B is an active past continuous; C uses the past tense 'gave' instead of the participle 'given'.
Trap: the passive needs the past participle (V3), not the past tense (V2).

q: Select all the sentences that are in the passive voice.
options: The children were playing in the park.
She has been working here for years.
solution:
A passive verb is a form of be + past participle, with the receiver of the action as subject.
B: 'were announced' — the results receive the action → passive. D: 'is being widened' — the highway receives the action → passive.
A: 'were playing' is be + V-ing (active past continuous). C: 'has been working' is an active present perfect continuous — the subject does the work.
Trap: the word 'been' alone does not make a verb passive; look for be + V3.

q:
The committee should consider the proposal carefully.
Passive: The proposal ______ carefully by the committee.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Modal + base verb (active) → modal + be + V3 (passive): should be considered.
A omits 'be'; B shifts the time to the past ('should have been considered' = it ought to have happened earlier); D uses the base form instead of the past participle.
Trap: modal passive = modal + be + V3.

q:
You ______ wear a helmet while riding a two-wheeler; it is required by law.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A legal requirement expresses obligation → must.
'may' and 'might' express permission or possibility; 'could' expresses ability or possibility — none conveys a compulsory rule.
Trap: 'it is required by law' is the clue for obligation.

q:
The lights in his office are still on at midnight, so he ______ be working late.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A confident deduction from evidence (lights on at midnight) uses must + base verb.
'can't' expresses impossibility, which contradicts the evidence; 'needn't' expresses lack of necessity, not deduction; 'ought' needs 'to' (ought to be) and expresses expectation or duty.
Trap: must (certain yes) vs can't (certain no).

q:
She ______ have left the office already; her bag is still on her desk.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The evidence (bag still on the desk) makes her leaving impossible in the speaker's judgement → can't have + V3 (negative deduction about the past).
'must have left' is a positive deduction that contradicts the evidence; 'should have left' means she was expected to leave but did not; 'needn't have left' means leaving was unnecessary — none fits.
Trap: past deduction — must have (sure yes), can't have (sure no).

q:
You ______ have brought an umbrella; it did not rain at all.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'needn't have + V3' means an action was done but was unnecessary — you brought it, but there was no need.
'mustn't have' is not a standard form for past deduction or obligation; 'can't have brought' would mean it is impossible that you brought it, which does not fit the speaker's point; 'wouldn't have brought' needs a condition (if …).
Trap: needn't have done (did it, but unnecessarily) ≠ didn't need to do (probably did not do it).

q:
When I was a child, I ______ climb that mango tree in a minute, but now I can't.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Ability in the past is expressed by could; the contrast 'but now I can't' confirms it.
'can' is present ability; 'must' is obligation or deduction; 'might' is possibility.
Trap: past ability = could / was able to.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
You ___(i)___ submit the form by Friday; it is compulsory. You ___(ii)___ attach a photograph if you wish, but it is optional. You ___(iii)___ fill in the form with a pencil, because pencil entries are rejected. If you have any doubt, you ___(iv)___ call the help desk.
solution:
(i) 'it is compulsory' → obligation: must.
(ii) 'optional' → permission: may.
(iii) Pencil entries are rejected → prohibition: must not.
(iv) An available option → can.
A swaps (i) and (ii). C uses 'need not' (= not necessary), which does not express a ban. D makes the optional photograph compulsory.
Trap: must not = prohibited; need not = not required.

q:
I ______ finish the report last night, so I couldn't go to the party.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Obligation in the past is expressed by had to; 'must' has no past form.
'must' and 'have to' are present forms that clash with 'last night'; 'should' expresses advice and cannot explain why I could not go.
Trap: must (now) → had to (past).

q:
You ______ to apologise to her for your rude remarks.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Of these modals only ought is followed by 'to' + base verb (ought to apologise).
'should', 'must' and 'had better' take the base verb directly ('should apologise', not 'should to apologise').
Trap: ought to, have to, used to — 'to' is part of the expression; should / must / had better have no 'to'.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: You had better to leave now.
They must to submit the report by Monday.
She dare not speak to the manager.
solution:
When 'need' and 'dare' are used as modals (in negatives and questions), they take the base verb without 'to' and no -s: 'He need not come', 'She dare not speak' — both correct.
A: 'had better' takes the base verb → had better leave. C: 'must' takes the base verb → must submit.
Trap: modal need/dare — no 'to', no -s; main-verb need — 'He does not need to come'.

q:
Nisha enjoys ______ to classical music in the evening.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'enjoy' is followed by a gerund (V-ing): enjoys listening.
'to listen' — 'enjoy' does not take a to-infinitive; 'listen' and 'listened' cannot follow 'enjoy'.
Trap: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, consider, deny, suggest + V-ing.

q:
We have decided ______ the trip to next month because of the exams.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'decide' is followed by a to-infinitive: decided to postpone.
'postponing' — 'decide' does not take a gerund; 'postpone' lacks 'to'; 'to postponing' mixes the infinitive marker with -ing.
Trap: decide, hope, agree, refuse, plan, manage + to V1.

q:
I am looking forward to ______ you at the conference next week.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
In 'look forward to', the word 'to' is a preposition, and a preposition is followed by a noun or a gerund → looking forward to meeting.
'meet', 'be meeting' and 'have met' treat 'to' as the infinitive marker.
Trap: look forward to, object to, be used to, with a view to + V-ing.

q:
Rajan stopped ______ after the doctor warned him about his lungs.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'stop + V-ing' = give up an activity → stopped smoking (he quit).
'stop + to-infinitive' = stop one activity in order to do another, so 'stopped to smoke' would mean he paused in order to smoke — the opposite of the intended meaning. 'smoke' and 'to smoking' are ungrammatical after 'stopped'.
Trap: stop / remember / forget / try change meaning with V-ing vs to-infinitive.

q:
The teacher made the students ______ the essay again.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'make', 'let' and 'help' (in the active voice) take object + bare infinitive (base verb without 'to'): made the students rewrite.
'to rewrite' adds 'to'; 'rewriting' and 'rewritten' do not fit this causative pattern with an active meaning.
Trap: make someone do (active), but 'The students were made to rewrite it' (passive).

q:
I clearly remember ______ him at a conference in Mysuru in 2019.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'remember + V-ing' refers to a memory of something that happened earlier → remember meeting him (in 2019).
'remember + to-infinitive' refers to a task still to be done ('Remember to meet him tomorrow'), which clashes with 'in 2019'; 'meet' and 'met' cannot follow 'remember' in this way.
Trap: remember doing (memory) vs remember to do (task).

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Ravi avoided ___(i)___ the reporter's question, but he agreed ___(ii)___ the documents. His lawyer advised him ___(iii)___ any statement, and Ravi could not help ___(iv)___ at the reporters' persistence.
options: (i) to answer (ii) signing (iii) not making (iv) to smile
(i) answering (ii) to sign (iii) not to make (iv) smiling
(i) answering (ii) signing (iii) not to make (iv) to smile
(i) answering (ii) to sign (iii) to not making (iv) smile
solution:
(i) avoid + V-ing → answering.
(ii) agree + to-infinitive → to sign.
(iii) advise + object + (not) to-infinitive → not to make.
(iv) can't/couldn't help + V-ing (= could not stop oneself) → smiling.
A fails (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv); C fails (ii) and (iv); D fails (iii) and (iv).
Trap: 'could not help to smile' is a common error.

q:
Having lived in Shimla for ten years, he is used to ______ in cold weather.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'be used to' (= be accustomed to) contains the preposition 'to', so it takes a gerund → is used to working.
'work' would confuse it with 'used to + V1' (a past habit: 'He used to work'); 'worked' and 'have worked' cannot follow a preposition.
Trap: be used to + V-ing (accustomed) vs used to + V1 (past habit).

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: She suggested going to the museum on Sunday.
He denied to have taken the money.
They are considering moving to Pune next year.
I let him to use my laptop for the test.
solution:
'suggest' and 'consider' are followed by a gerund → suggested going, considering moving — A and C are correct.
B: 'deny' takes a gerund → denied taking (or having taken) the money.
D: 'let' takes object + bare infinitive → let him use.
Trap: suggest / consider / deny + V-ing; let / make + object + V1.

q:
The doctor advised him ______ sugar and fried food.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'advise + object + to-infinitive': advised him to avoid.
'advised him avoiding' — with a personal object, 'advise' needs the to-infinitive ('advised avoiding' is possible only without an object); 'avoid' lacks 'to'; 'for avoiding' is not a pattern of 'advise'.
Trap: advise / tell / ask / order + someone + to V1.

q:
Your sister is a doctor, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A positive statement takes a negative tag made from the same auxiliary and tense: 'is' → isn't she.
'is she' is positive after a positive statement; 'doesn't she' uses the wrong auxiliary; 'wasn't she' changes the tense.
Trap: tag = same auxiliary, same tense, opposite polarity, pronoun subject.

q:
They went to the market yesterday, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The statement is a positive simple past with no auxiliary, so the tag uses 'did' in the negative → didn't they.
'weren't they' uses 'be', which is not in the statement; 'did they' is positive; 'don't they' is present tense.
Trap: no auxiliary in the statement ⇒ use do / does / did in the tag.

q:
Nobody called while I was out, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'Nobody' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive; indefinite pronouns for people (nobody, everyone, someone) are picked up by 'they' in the tag → did they.
'didn't they' and 'didn't he' are negative tags after a negative statement; 'was it' uses the wrong auxiliary and pronoun.
Trap: never / nobody / nothing / hardly make the statement negative.

q:
I am late again, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The standard negative tag for 'I am' is aren't I (in very formal style, 'am I not').
'am not I' has the wrong word order; 'isn't it' changes the subject; 'don't I' uses an auxiliary that is not in the statement.
Trap: 'amn't I' is non-standard; use 'aren't I'.

q:
Let's go for a walk after dinner, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A suggestion beginning with 'Let's' (= let us, including the speaker) takes the tag shall we.
'will you' and 'won't you' are tags for commands or requests addressed to someone else; 'don't we' is not used with 'Let's'.
Trap: Let's …, shall we? — but an imperative such as 'Open the door, will you?'

q:
He hardly ever visits his parents, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'hardly ever' gives the statement a negative meaning, so the tag is positive; the verb 'visits' is simple present → does he.
'doesn't he' treats the statement as positive; 'is he' uses the wrong auxiliary; 'did he' changes the tense.
Trap: hardly, scarcely, seldom, rarely, never → positive tag.

q:
Please open the window, ______?
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
An imperative (a command or request) addressed to the listener takes the tag will you (also 'would you' / 'won't you').
'shall we' and 'don't we' include the speaker and belong with suggestions such as 'Let's …'; 'do you' is not used after an imperative.
Trap: imperative → will you; Let's → shall we.

q: Select all the sentences in which the question tag is correct.
options: You have never been to Ladakh, haven't you?
There is a problem with the server, isn't there?
Neither of them came to the party, did they?
Meena can't drive a car, can't she?
solution:
B: 'there is' is repeated in the tag with 'there' → isn't there — correct.
C: 'neither' makes the statement negative → positive tag; 'neither of them' is picked up by 'they' → did they — correct.
A: 'never' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive → have you?
D: a negative statement needs a positive tag → can she?
Trap: negative words (never, neither, nobody, hardly) flip the tag to positive.

q:
In her free time, Lata likes reading, painting and ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Items joined in a list must have the same grammatical form (parallelism). 'reading' and 'painting' are gerunds → swimming.
'to swim' is an infinitive, 'swim' a base verb and 'she swims' a clause — each breaks the pattern.
Trap: check the form of the first item in a list.

q:
The new manager is efficient, ______ and approachable.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The list is of adjectives describing the manager (efficient, ___, approachable) → honest.
'honesty' is a noun; 'with honesty' is a prepositional phrase; 'has honesty' is a verb phrase — each breaks the parallel structure.
Trap: adjective, adjective and adjective.

q: Which one of the following sentences is correctly constructed?
options: He not only plays the guitar but also the violin.
Not only he plays the guitar but also the violin.
He plays not only the guitar but also the violin.
He plays not only the guitar but also plays the violin.
solution:
With correlative pairs, the words after each half must be parallel. In C, 'not only' and 'but also' are each followed by a noun phrase (the guitar / the violin) — correct.
A: 'not only' precedes a verb ('plays') but 'but also' precedes a noun. B: a sentence-initial 'not only' needs inversion ('Not only does he play …'). D: 'not only' + noun, but 'but also' + verb.
Trap: place 'not only' immediately before the first of the two matching elements.

q:
The training covers how to write code, how to test it, and ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The first two items are 'how to + verb' phrases, so the third must match → how to deploy it.
'deploying it' (gerund phrase), 'the deployment of it' (noun phrase) and 'to deploy it' (infinitive without 'how') break the parallel series.
Trap: repeat the structure of the earlier items exactly.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct and has a parallel structure?
options: The committee was asked to review the budget, to cut costs and that it should report by Friday.
The committee was asked reviewing the budget, to cut costs and reporting by Friday.
The committee was asked to review the budget, cutting costs and to report by Friday.
The committee was asked to review the budget, cut costs and report by Friday.
solution:
After 'was asked to', the three tasks must share one form. In D, one 'to' governs three base verbs — review, cut, report — which is correct parallelism.
A switches from infinitives to a 'that' clause. B mixes gerunds with an infinitive (and 'asked reviewing' is itself wrong). C puts a gerund between two infinitives.
Trap: one 'to' can serve the whole list: to review, cut and report.

q:
Ankit prefers walking to ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The pattern is prefer + V-ing + to + V-ing; here 'to' is a preposition and the two activities must be parallel → prefers walking to driving.
'drive' and 'drives' are not gerunds; 'to drive' would give 'to to drive'.
Trap: prefer A to B (both nouns or gerunds); but 'would rather walk than drive'.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
The job requires (i) / a sharp analytical mind, (ii) / good communication skills (iii) / and to be patient. (iv)
solution:
The verb 'requires' takes a list of noun phrases: a sharp analytical mind, good communication skills and … The last item, 'to be patient', is an infinitive and breaks the parallel structure → it should be 'patience'. Part (iv) is wrong.
(i)–(iii) are correct noun-phrase items.
Trap: in a list, the last item is where parallelism most often breaks.

q:
Her duties include answering calls, scheduling meetings and ______.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
options: the maintenance of office files is
solution:
The list consists of gerund phrases (answering calls, scheduling meetings), so the third item must be a gerund phrase → maintaining the office files.
'to maintain …' is an infinitive; 'maintains …' is a finite verb; the last option adds a second verb 'is', making the sentence ungrammatical.
Trap: gerund, gerund and gerund.

q: Select all the sentences that are grammatically correct and have a parallel structure.
options: She is admired for her kindness, her honesty and her generosity.
The new phone is cheap, light and it is easy to use.
You can travel to Goa by bus, by train or by air.
He likes to read novels and watching old films.
solution:
A: three parallel noun phrases (her kindness, her honesty, her generosity) — correct.
C: three parallel prepositional phrases (by bus, by train, by air) — correct.
B: two adjectives followed by a clause ('it is easy to use') → cheap, light and easy to use.
D: an infinitive paired with a gerund → 'to read … and (to) watch' or 'reading … and watching'.
Trap: items joined by 'and / or' share one form.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
Each of the students (i) / have submitted (ii) / the assignment (iii) / before the deadline. (iv)
solution:
'Each of the students' has the singular subject 'each', so the verb must be singular → has submitted. Part (ii) is wrong.
(i) is the correct subject phrase; (iii) and (iv) are correct.
Trap: the plural 'students' next to the verb is bait — the subject is 'each'.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
If I would have (i) / known about the meeting, (ii) / I would have (iii) / attended it. (iv)
solution:
In a third conditional, the if-clause takes the past perfect ('If I had known'); 'would' never appears in the if-clause. Part (i) is wrong.
(ii) completes the condition; (iii)–(iv) 'I would have attended it' is the correct result clause.
Trap: 'would have' belongs to the result clause only.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
The scenery (i) / of the hill station (ii) / are breathtaking (iii) / during the monsoon. (iv)
solution:
'scenery' is an uncountable singular noun and is the real subject; 'of the hill station' only describes it. The verb must be singular → is breathtaking. Part (iii) is wrong.
(i), (ii) and (iv) are correct.
Trap: scenery, furniture, luggage, information — singular, with no plural form.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
He has been working (i) / with this firm (ii) / as a senior analyst (iii) / for 2015. (iv)
solution:
'2015' is a point in time; with a perfect tense it needs 'since' (since 2015). 'for' is used with a period (for nine years). Part (iv) is wrong.
(i) 'has been working' correctly shows an action continuing up to now; (ii) and (iii) are correct.
Trap: since + point, for + period.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
She gave me (i) / many useful informations (ii) / about the (iii) / admission process. (iv)
solution:
'information' is uncountable: it has no plural and does not take 'many' → 'much useful information' or 'a lot of useful information'. Part (ii) is wrong.
(i), (iii) and (iv) are correct.
Trap: informations, advices, furnitures, luggages are all incorrect.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
My friend did not (i) / knew the answer (ii) / to the last question (iii) / in the quiz. (iv)
solution:
After the auxiliary 'did' (and 'did not'), the main verb is in the base form: did not know. Part (ii) is wrong.
(i) 'did not' already carries the past tense; (iii) and (iv) are correct.
Trap: the past tense is shown only once — on 'did'.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
Scarcely had (i) / the train left the platform (ii) / than a passenger (iii) / pulled the emergency chain. (iv)
solution:
'Scarcely' pairs with 'when' (Scarcely had … when …); 'than' belongs with 'no sooner'. Part (iii) is wrong.
(i) correctly inverts the auxiliary after the negative opener; (ii) and (iv) are correct.
Trap: had the sentence begun 'No sooner had …', 'than' would be right — always check the opener.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
The manager, along with (i) / his two assistants, (ii) / were present (iii) / at the annual meeting. (iv)
solution:
'along with his two assistants' is an add-on phrase; the subject is 'The manager' (singular) → was present. Part (iii) is wrong.
(i), (ii) and (iv) are correct.
Trap: along with / as well as / together with do not make the subject plural.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
The board said that neither (i) / of the two proposals were (ii) / acceptable in (iii) / its present form. (iv)
solution:
