'Neither of + plural noun' takes a singular verb because 'neither' means 'not either one' → neither of the two proposals was acceptable. Part (ii) is wrong.
(i) 'said that neither' is correct; (iii) is correct; (iv) 'its' correctly refers to the singular 'neither (proposal)'.
Trap: neither of / either of / each of → singular verb.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
Hardly I had reached (i) / the station (ii) / when the train (iii) / started moving. (iv)
solution:
A negative adverb ('Hardly') at the start of a clause requires inversion: Hardly had I reached … Part (i) is wrong.
(ii) is correct; (iii) correctly pairs 'hardly' with 'when'; (iv) is a correct simple past.
Trap: the pair hardly … when is right here — the error is the missing inversion, not the connector.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
My cousin is (i) / more cleverer (ii) / than her (iii) / younger brother. (iv)
solution:
A comparative takes only one marker; 'more cleverer' combines 'more' with '-er' (a double comparative) → 'cleverer' or 'more clever'. Part (ii) is wrong.
(i), (iii) and (iv) are correct; 'younger' is a correct comparative before a noun.
Trap: more better, more cleverer, most cleverest — all double markers.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
Each of the (i) / engineers who (ii) / work on this project (iii) / have to sign the register daily. (iv)
solution:
There are two verbs. 'who work' agrees with its antecedent 'engineers' (plural) — correct. The main verb belongs to the subject 'Each', which is singular → has to sign. Part (iv) is wrong.
(i) and (ii) correctly form the subject and begin the relative clause; (iii) is correct for the reason above.
Trap: seeing 'Each', a careless reader 'corrects' (iii) to 'works' — but the relative clause follows 'engineers', not 'each'.

q:
Which one of the numbered parts of the following sentence contains a grammatical error?
All the old furniture were (i) / replaced last year (ii) / because the rooms (iii) / were being renovated. (iv)
solution:
'furniture' is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb even after 'all' → All the old furniture was replaced. Part (i) is wrong.
(ii) is a correct time phrase; (iii)–(iv) 'the rooms were being renovated' is a correct plural past continuous passive.
Trap: 'all' does not make an uncountable noun plural.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
solution:
With a third-person singular subject, the negative simple present is does not (doesn't) + base verb: She doesn't like.
B uses 'don't' with 'she'; C marks the tense twice ('doesn't likes'); D has no auxiliary.
Trap: after does / doesn't / did, the verb is in its base form.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?
options: The furniture in the hall is new.
He gave me some good advice.
I have lost my luggages at the airport.
The news from the hospital is encouraging.
solution:
'luggage' is uncountable; it has no plural form → 'my luggage' (or 'my bags'). So C is incorrect.
A: 'furniture … is' — uncountable, singular, correct. B: 'some good advice' — uncountable without 'a', correct. D: 'news … is' — singular, correct.
Trap: uncountable nouns: no -s, no 'a', singular verb.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: She laid on the sofa all afternoon.
She lay on the sofa all afternoon.
She lied on the sofa all afternoon.
She has laid on the sofa all afternoon.
solution:
'lie' (= rest in a flat position) is intransitive: lie – lay – lain. Its past tense is 'lay': She lay on the sofa.
A: 'laid' is the past of the transitive 'lay' (= put something down) and needs an object. C: 'lied' is the past of 'lie' (= tell an untruth). D: the present perfect of 'lie' (rest) is 'has lain', not 'has laid'.
Trap: lay (put) – laid – laid; lie (rest) – lay – lain; lie (untruth) – lied – lied.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: I have seen him at the market yesterday.
I have saw him at the market yesterday.
I was seen him at the market yesterday.
I saw him at the market yesterday.
solution:
A finished past time ('yesterday') requires the simple past: I saw him.
A uses the present perfect with a finished past time, which is not allowed. B combines 'have' with the past tense 'saw' instead of 'seen'. C uses the passive 'was seen' with an object, which is ungrammatical.
Trap: yesterday / ago / last week → simple past, never the present perfect.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: Neither Ravi nor his friends were invited to the wedding.
The committee has submitted its report.
The cattle is grazing in the field.
Five kilometres is too far to walk in this heat.
solution:
A: with neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'his friends' → were — correct.
B: 'its report' shows the committee acting as one body, so the singular 'has' is consistent — correct.
D: a distance taken as one amount is singular → 'is too far' — correct.
C: 'cattle' is always plural → 'The cattle are grazing'.
Trap: cattle, police, people — plural without -s.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?
options: Arjun is the tallest boy in the class.
Arjun is taller than any other boy in the class.
No other boy in the class is as tall as Arjun.
Arjun is taller than all the boys in the class.
solution:
When the person compared belongs to the group, the comparison must exclude him: 'taller than any other boy' or 'than all the other boys'. D compares Arjun with a group that includes himself, which is illogical, so D is incorrect.
A (superlative), B (comparative with 'any other') and C (positive degree with 'no other … as … as') are the three correct ways to say the same thing.
Trap: superlative ⇔ comparative + 'any other' ⇔ 'no other … as … as'.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Despite the heavy rain, the match continued.
Despite of the heavy rain, the match continued.
In spite the heavy rain, the match continued.
Despite it rained heavily, the match continued.
solution:
'despite' is a preposition used without 'of' and followed by a noun phrase: Despite the heavy rain — correct.
B adds 'of' to 'despite'. C drops 'of' from 'in spite of'. D puts a clause after 'despite' (use 'Although it rained heavily …').
Trap: despite = in spite of; never 'despite of'.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Walking along the beach, a shell caught my eye.
Walking along the beach, I noticed a shell.
While walking along the beach, the shell was noticed by me.
Walking along the beach, the shell looked beautiful.
solution:
An opening participial phrase ('Walking along the beach') describes the subject of the main clause, so that subject must be the person who walked. In B the subject 'I' did the walking — correct.
A, C and D attach the phrase to 'a shell' / 'the shell', which says the shell was walking (a dangling modifier).
Trap: ask 'who is walking?' — the answer must be the subject right after the comma.

q: Select all the grammatically correct sentences.
options: If he will come early, I will tell him the news.
I will wait here until she will return.
If I were you, I would accept the offer.
Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the last bus.
solution:
C: a second conditional (unreal present) takes 'were' in the if-clause and 'would + V1' in the main clause — correct.
A: no 'will' in an if-clause → 'If he comes early'.
B: no 'will' in a time clause after 'until' → 'until she returns'.
D: 'unless' already means 'if not', so 'unless … not' is a double negative → 'Unless you hurry'.
Trap: an MSQ may have only one correct option — judge each sentence on its own.

q: Which one of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: It being a rainy day, the school remained closed.
Being a rainy day, the school remained closed.
Being rainy day, the school remained closed.
It was a rainy day, the school remained closed.
solution:
A participial phrase with its own subject ('It being a rainy day') is an absolute construction and can stand before any main clause — A is correct.
B: without 'It', the phrase 'Being a rainy day' attaches to 'the school', saying the school was a rainy day (dangling modifier). C repeats that error and also drops the article. D joins two complete sentences with only a comma (comma splice); it needs 'so' or a semicolon.
Trap: an opening participle must either describe the main subject or carry its own subject.

In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
The committee ___(i)___ its decision only after the members ___(ii)___ the report, ___(iii)___ the chairman, who ___(iv)___ on leave, could not attend the final meeting.
options: (i) has announced (ii) had studied (iii) but (iv) were
solution:
(i) A completed past action in a past narrative → announced.
(ii) The earlier of two past actions ('only after') → past perfect had studied.
(iii) Contrast between the members' work and the chairman's absence → but.
(iv) 'who' refers to 'the chairman' (singular) → was.
B fails (ii) (present perfect in a past narrative). C fails (i) (present perfect clashing with 'had studied') and (iv). D fails (iv) ('the chairman … were').
Shortcut: (iv) removes C and D; (ii) removes B.

In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
___(i)___ the heavy traffic, Meena reached ___(ii)___ airport an hour early, ___(iii)___ her flight had already been rescheduled, so she had to wait ___(iv)___ the lounge for three hours.
solution:
(i) A preposition of contrast before a noun phrase → Despite (never 'despite of'; 'although' needs a clause).
(ii) The particular airport she was flying from → the.
(iii) Reaching early contrasts with the flight being rescheduled → but.
(iv) An enclosed space → wait in the lounge.
A fails (i) and (ii); C fails (i); D fails (ii) and (iv).
Trap: of 'despite' and 'in spite of', only the second takes 'of'.

In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Each of the volunteers ___(i)___ a medical kit, and the kits ___(ii)___ distributed ___(iii)___ the camp began. By evening, the volunteers ___(iv)___ over two hundred patients.
options: (i) were given (ii) was (iii) before (iv) have examined
(i) was given (ii) was (iii) before (iv) had examined
(i) was given (ii) were (iii) before (iv) had examined
solution:
(i) 'Each of' → singular: was given.
(ii) 'the kits' is plural: were distributed.
(iii) The distribution came earlier than the start of the camp → before.
(iv) 'By evening' (a past point) → past perfect had examined.
A fails (i), (ii) and (iv). B fails (ii). C fails (iii) ('distributed until the camp began' is illogical) and (iv) ('by evening' needs a perfect tense).
Trap: 'by + past time' ⇒ past perfect.

In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
She is ___(i)___ honest woman ___(ii)___ never tells ___(iii)___ lie, and she is respected ___(iv)___ everyone in the village.
solution:
(i) 'honest' has a silent h → an.
(ii) Subject of 'tells', referring to a person → who.
(iii) 'lie' is a singular countable noun, non-specific, beginning with a consonant sound → a lie.
(iv) The doer in a passive sentence is introduced by by.
A fails (i) and (ii); B fails (ii), (iii) and (iv); D fails (iii) and (iv).
Trap: tell a lie / tell the truth.

In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
The guide told us that the fort ___(i)___ by a local king four centuries earlier and that we ___(ii)___ not take photographs inside. He asked us ___(iii)___ we had bought tickets and told us ___(iv)___ the murals.
options: (i) has been built (ii) can (iii) whether (iv) not to touch
(i) had been built (ii) could (iii) whether (iv) not to touch
(i) had been built (ii) could (iii) that (iv) to not touching
(i) had built (ii) could (iii) whether (iv) not to touch
solution:
This is reported speech after the past verb 'told':
(i) An event earlier than the telling, in the passive (built by a king) → had been built.
(ii) 'cannot' back-shifts to could (not).
(iii) A reported yes/no question → whether (or if).
(iv) A reported prohibition → told us not to touch.
A keeps present forms (no back-shift). C uses 'that' for a question and the ungrammatical 'to not touching'. D uses the active 'had built', which would make the fort the builder.
Trap: check voice as well as tense in reported clauses.

In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
If the alarm ___(i)___ on time last night, the guard ___(ii)___ the intruder. Since it did not, the police now ___(iii)___ to rely on CCTV footage, which ___(iv)___ being examined at present.
options: (i) had gone off (ii) could have stopped (iii) have (iv) is
(i) went off (ii) could stop (iii) has (iv) are
(i) had gone off (ii) could have stopped (iii) has (iv) is
(i) would have gone off (ii) could have stopped (iii) have (iv) are
solution:
(i), (ii) An unreal past condition ('Since it did not' confirms it) is a third conditional: had gone off … could have stopped.
(iii) 'police' is always plural → have.
(iv) 'which' refers to 'footage' (uncountable, singular) → is being examined.
B uses a second conditional for a past event and fails (iii) and (iv). C fails (iii) ('the police has'). D puts 'would' in the if-clause and fails (iv).
Trap: police → plural; footage → singular.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
The team captain, as well as the players, ___(i)___ confident. Everyone in the squad ___(ii)___ trained hard, and the coach says the squad is ready to defend ___(iii)___ title. It is the players ___(iv)___ deserve the credit.
solution:
(i) 'as well as the players' is an add-on; the subject is 'The team captain' → is.
(ii) 'Everyone' is singular → has trained.
(iii) 'the squad is ready' treats the squad as one unit → its title (possessive, no apostrophe).
(iv) Subject of 'deserve', referring to people → who.
A fails (i) and (ii). C fails (ii) and (iv). D fails (iii) ('it's' = it is) and (iv) ('which' for people).
Trap: keep the number consistent — 'the squad is … its'.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Despite ___(i)___ no training in electronics, Kiran insisted ___(ii)___ the old radio himself. He succeeded ___(iii)___ it, but forgot ___(iv)___ the power supply before opening it again, and got a mild shock.
options: (i) to have (ii) on repairing (iii) to fix (iv) switching off
(i) having (ii) to repair (iii) in fixing (iv) switching off
(i) having (ii) on repairing (iii) in fixing (iv) to switch off
(i) having (ii) on repairing (iii) in fixing (iv) switch off
solution:
(i) A preposition ('despite') is followed by a gerund → having.
(ii) insist on + V-ing → on repairing.
(iii) succeed in + V-ing → in fixing.
(iv) forget + to-infinitive = fail to do something one should do → to switch off; 'forgot switching off' would mean he forgot a past act of switching off.
A fails (i), (iii) and (iv); B fails (ii) and (iv); D fails (iv) (bare 'switch off' after 'forgot').
Trap: forget / remember + to V1 = a task; + V-ing = a memory.
